title: Clinic appointment booking
brief: A group of 60 clinics lets patients find a free slot, book it and get a text reminder. Slots open at 8 am, and the phone lines used to melt. Two people must never get the same slot, and reminders must go out even when the text-message company has a bad hour.

clarify.q: Can two patients hold the same slot?
clarify.a: Never. A double booking means a patient turns up and there is no room for them, so a booked slot must be recorded exactly once.

clarify.q: Do reminders have to arrive instantly?
clarify.a: No. A reminder a few minutes late is fine, but it must not be lost. That means it can wait in a line.

clarify.q: How busy is the 8 am rush?
clarify.a: About six times a normal busy hour, for around ten minutes, when new slots open.
Yes. Records are private, so every booking is tied to a signed-in patient.

notes: Peak means the busiest minute of a normal weekday, approx.
A reminder text costs about a cent; the cost line is small but real.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

hints: Reminders are not urgent. What lets the work wait without losing it?
Put a queue and a small worker pool between your servers and the text-message service, so a slow provider does not slow patients.
A booking must be exact, so keep slots in a database with transactions and two copies across zones. Add a cache for browsing, and a search index so slot search does not hit the main database.

editorial.summary: This is a small, correct system. Browsing is the bulk of the traffic and can be cached; the booking itself is a few requests per second and goes to a real transactional database. Reminders are the only work that talks to an outside company, so they ride a queue.

designs.name: Cached browsing, queued reminders
designs.why: The load balancer spreads patients across three servers in two zones. A cache answers most browsing, a search index answers slot searches, and the SQL database (two copies, synchronous) holds the slots. Reminders wait in a queue so the text provider can be slow or capped without hurting patients.

tradeoffs: Synchronous replication makes every booking a few milliseconds slower, but a zone failure can never lose or double a booking.
A 60-second cache keeps the database calm but may show a slot that was just taken; the booking step checks again, so nobody is double booked.
The queue adds a short delay to reminders, and in return a text-provider problem never touches patients.
The search index is a copy of the slots, so search can be a few seconds behind. It costs extra but keeps search off the main database.
editorial.realWorld: Online booking tools for clinic groups commonly handle a few hundred requests a second at the daily peak, and most of that is people looking, not booking (approx.). Text reminders are usually sent through an outside provider that caps how fast you can send.

correctness.prompt: Two people book the last available slot at once. What schema constraint and transaction would allow only one booking?
correctness.discussion: Identify the scarce resource and time range. Enforce uniqueness for fixed slots, or prevent overlapping reservations with a database constraint or serializable transaction. Check availability and create the reservation atomically in the authoritative store. Cached availability is only a hint. Give each booking request a stable key so retries return the original booking rather than consume another slot.

fields.label: Two requests read the last available slot; one commits, then loses its reply. What protects the retry?
options: A cached availability check before each insert
A unique reservation key and an atomic conditional claim in the authoritative store
fields.explanation: The committed reservation owns the resource. Retrying its stable key returns the same reservation; an independent read and insert can oversell.

fields.label: The first claim committed before the second request reaches the store. What must the second request do?
options: Reject that claim or offer another slot without decrementing inventory again
Accept it because both requests originally saw availability
fields.explanation: Only the atomic check at commit can allocate the last resource. A stale search result is not ownership.
